utterances.text: Now, you have read the first paragraph of this particular letter to Colonel Morillon. What is your view of that particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: My opinion is that it was not true, and I was on site myself because I went on site, from Travnik and Guca Gora, I visited then. In my opinion, I think this was an extension of the propaganda. It's the same thing. Whereas we had told the local people that these allegations were not grounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, Mate Boban, in this letter, makes reference to the desecration of certain Catholic monasteries and religious sites. Tell me the reaction, if you will, to the Bosnian Muslim military leadership when receiving allegations of this type?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I remember that once, after the incident in Guca Gora, that we had to go visit General Alagic and report these accusations, saying that in the Guca Gora church several weeks before, certain sacred objects had been damaged. General Alagic was impressed by the accusations, he apologised immediately, and said to us immediately that he would have this kind of activity stopped immediately, that he would attempt to track down the guilty parties in order to punish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you contrast the degree of damage done to Catholic religious sites in Muslim-held territory versus the amount of damage and the scale of damage done to Muslim religious sites in HVO-held territory?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The Catholic objects were practically never damaged. I saw one minor example in a Catholic church near Busovaca. There, there was a little bit of damage to the church. I saw many examples of mosques, minarets, including others in Ahmici, where the mosque and minaret had been completely destroyed. This also happened in other places. The ratio between the damage to Catholic buildings as opposed to Muslim buildings was something really that one cannot say was comparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you've described the reaction of General Alagic to getting information that Catholic sites had been destroyed or damaged. Can you tell the Judges the reaction of HVO officers in respect of claims that Muslim sites had been damaged or destroyed by their forces?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, the allegations, first of all, were submitted to find out their immediate reaction to these, and in my experience, we found that the reaction of the HVO military personnel was of general disinterest or they would simply deny or put these accusations onto the backs of "uncontrolled elements," as they called them. At times they would promise to carry out an investigation, but there was never any report of any type of such an investigation being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, that concludes the presentation of evidence in respect of the propaganda and related issues. I'll now turn to a different subject, and that is: Colonel Morsink, can you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here because you said you've just completed, but we have a prior obligation, so we will resume at 2.45. Thank you very much. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.34 p.m. 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume our hearing now. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, Mr. Hayman, I believe we are supposed to finish with this witness this afternoon, including the cross-examination. There are interpretation problems, and we have to accept the fact that they exist and we try to be as concise as we can. We only have reached Point 3 out of 13, and so we have to try to focus things, to make things short because there's got to be a cross-examination, there are technical problems which just exist, and that's what happens, and we can't do anything about it. We'll take the time we need. I spoke to Maja, our wonderful chief of service. If necessary, we'll even work until 7.00, but we'll shorten, if necessary, the break, we'll take extra time now because we were talking about that issue, but I say very clearly that I insist upon the cross-examination being completed this afternoon. We will stay as long as we need. You must also understand that there are administrative and organisational problems as well. Justice is eternal, but alas, alas, there are human problems that come into play as well. Mr. Harmon, let me remind you that we are only on Point 3, we finished with the HVO propaganda, I noted that there are 13 points. If you want to deal with them with the same care, which is praiseworthy and legitimate in your opinion, that means we're going to have him here for two days. Can we afford this luxury? I'm not sure that we can. There you go. And, of course, there's the cross-examination, I know that it's going to be an important one, and I do not want to limit the rights of the Defence, I say very clearly, I do not want to limit the Defence's rights. The accused has the right to explore all defence opportunities available to him. You know, Mr. Harmon, that when the Prosecutor takes a long time then the cross-examination is long as well. That is obvious. What I say to you I will say in a few weeks to the Defence, when you have a long examination-in-chief, then you have a long cross-examination and the Judges ask a lot of questions about it. You know justice is a human affair, and even if we try to make it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It is not the Court's fault, it is the problem of interpreters. So if the problem was not to translate from Dutch to English and French, there would be no problem, in case you want to take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand that, Judge Riad, and thank you, I will try to expedite my examination, but obviously with the use of a Dutch interpreter, it slows proceedings down. But nevertheless, let me begin, and if I can very quickly turn to an electronic exhibit and have that immediately put on the screen. Mr. President, I'm going to return briefly to the previous testimony in Guca Gora on the mission in which Colonel Morsink went to Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, you testified in your direct examination that when you went to investigate claims that Croat villages had been burned in and around Guca Gora on the 8th of June, you found a village that was, in fact, burning and, in fact, it was a Muslim village, not a Croat village. Is the picture in front of you a picture that you took on the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This is a photograph which I took on the 8th or the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you see the village of Bandol burning?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it clearly. To the right, in front of the vehicle to the right. Right on the horizon you can see smoke and you can see burning houses. That is, I think, the village of Bandol.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And that is a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it's a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have that, Mr. Dubuisson, marked as an exhibit, however that is done electronically or otherwise, and I will continue with my examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It will be given a number, 419.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Morsink, let me ask you, can you please characterise the differences in the degree of cooperation between the Bosnian Muslim army and the HVO army in respect of investigating allegations of serious violations of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I have already given you a series of examples about collaboration with the Muslims, with the Muslim armed forces. For example, in Guca Gora, where the division commander promised to carry out an investigation. In Grahovcici, the third corps allowed us to have a meeting, and on the HVO side, things were very different. Ordinarily, we had no escort. In some exceptional cases, Mr. Jusic would accompany us, but in most of the cases, there was no escort, and we were stopped at each roadblock. When we protested, we had to go back to headquarters, we had to ask for authorisation again, sometimes it worked, sometimes it didn't. An example when it would never work was in Kruscica. There were cases when there was an HVO authorisation saying that we could be escorted from Travnik to Zenica, there would be a large group of wounded that had been chosen in the hospital, wounded people from all the groups, and despite all authorisations, we still had to stop at the HVO checkpoints. After an hour of talking, we would be sent back, and then there were authorisations for investigations which were granted each time, but in my opinion, these investigations never took place. We were promised investigations, but we never saw any results. And so we were given a lot of promises but there were very few results.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, did you attempt to investigate Gomionica and can you tell the Judges what response you received from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: When we were in Kiseljak, we heard rumours, according to which there had been fighting around that village, and that we were -- that the Muslim houses were being set on fire. We asked for authorisation to go there, and when we arrived, we were stopped at a roadblock near the front-line where the Canadian escort was also stopped. The Canadians were unable to get us through that roadblock. The HVO soldiers refused to authorise the passage. An argument that was used very often that is that it was too dangerous for us to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now let me turn to events that took place -- let me start with Ahmici. You were aware, since you arrived on the 16th of April, 1993, of a serious massacre that had occurred in the village of Ahmici. Were you ever provided, as a representative of ECMM, with any investigation results that had been conducted by the HVO into the circumstances of the massacre at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect to the truck bomb that occurred in Stari Vitez where Mario Cerkez said he was going to conduct an investigation, when you were in theatre, did you ever receive an investigation report from the HVO about the circumstances of that truck bombing?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of a shelling in Zenica that took place on the 19th of April, 1993, in which a significant number of civilians were killed, did you ever receive an investigation report or the result of any investigation from the HVO in respect of that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There were never any results from the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about General Alagic. General Alagic accompanied you on an investigation in respect of claims made about atrocities committed against the Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And General Alagic had an equivalent position to that held by Colonel Blaskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic ever accompany you on any of your investigations?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, he never went with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were any investigations, to your knowledge, ever conducted into violations relating to the forced use of civilians, Muslim civilians, to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We were promised that several times, but I never saw any result from any inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were any investigations, to your knowledge, ever conducted by the HVO into allegations about the intentional setting afire of Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I never got any results at all in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to a different topic, and that is interference with humanitarian aid by the HVO. Let me ask you this first question that calls merely for a "Yes" or "No" answer. While you were in Central Bosnia, did the HVO interfere with the delivery of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were in Central Bosnia, were you not, on the 10th of June when the Convoy of Joy was attacked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I don't want you to go into any details in that incident because we have already had significant testimony about that event here, but did you see the aftermath of that particular attack on that humanitarian aid convoy?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I saw damage and things had been stolen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you give us other examples when the HVO interfered with the delivery of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: An example where I myself, was when there was an attempt to bring humanitarian aid to Kruscica, from the end of May, Kruscica had been cut off from the surroundings, the immediate surroundings. For us and for the British battalion, there was no contact. We tried almost to go there almost every day, that is to Kruscica. We had daily contacts with the brigade commander, Mr. Cerkez, and the answer which we were always given was that the road was blocked by furious civilians that they could not control. We insisted that the road be opened, and even through the -- even through the assistance of the mayor, we weren't able to get through -- we were not able to achieve any concrete results. In the end, Mr. Blaskic sent an order, and in the order, he said that the road was to be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me interrupt you right there. If I could have two exhibits, please? The first exhibit would be Defence Exhibit 141. Can that be placed on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would prefer the witness not be interrupted. He was answering the question. Counsel apparently wants to stop him and direct his attention to a document before he completes his answer. We think the appropriate procedure is to allow him to complete, if the answer is responsive, and then go from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I disagree with Counsel. I appreciate being able to conduct my examination in the way that it's been conducted in the past. The witness referred to an exhibit -- to an order, the Defence has introduced the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Within certain limits, Mr. Harmon, however. If you ask a question, it would be proper for the witness to be able to answer all the way to the end. You can't do everything and everything here and everything there. You can't ask a question -- if you ask a question, you have to wait for an answer. The final word lies with the Judges, after all. I'm trying to be pleasant about this. Either you ask a question or you don't. If you do, you have to wait for the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, fine. I will defer showing the witness this exhibit. He will testify to the conclusion of his testimony, and then I will ask to show him two exhibits. Mr. Usher, we'll wait for a minute with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please, Colonel Morsink, if you continue with your evidence and then I will show you the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: On the 21st of June, the order arrived from Mr. Blaskic. It was an order that the road be opened and that the humanitarian convoys be allowed to go through. I accompanied the transport with the UNHCR. And to my great surprise, a second road was opened up as well, a road which was under HVO control. We were able to move the humanitarian aid for an hour. During that hour, we also had to treat the casualties, we had a physician with us, in order to treat the wounded. That's all I have to say for the first example. Another important example --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there because I have some questions to clarify your previous testimony. Now if we could show the witness Exhibit -- Defence Exhibit 141 and place that on the ELMO, please. Is there an English translation with that exhibit? Will you place that in front of the witness, please, Mr. Usher. Colonel Morsink, is this a copy of the order that you were just testifying about?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you receive this order from the British battalion?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I received that from the British battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, a couple points about this order. First of all, in the first paragraph, it refers to -- it's a command that orders -- the aid delivery to the village of Kruscica on the 21st of June, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned just a few minutes ago in your testimony that there was a secondary road through which you delivered aid; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. The main road had been barricaded by angry civilians, and after this order, another road was opened for us because -- the second was therefore made available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, was that secondary road made available five weeks earlier when you started your request to make and deliver aid to Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We weren't aware that there was another road. We had demanded authorisation to go to Kruscica every single day and we were always answered the same way: The road's being blocked by dissatisfied civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And then five weeks later you were informed of a secondary road through which you could deliver aid?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in respect of going to Kruscica to deliver aid, was your life threatened by an HVO officer and can you tell the Court about that, please?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: On the 9th of June, when I visited the HVO hospital in Nova Bila, the physicians told me that there were wounded people everywhere. They let me see the wounded people. And during the visit, I was suddenly confronted by an HVO officer. The officer, this HVO officer, whose photograph I have shown you this morning, was extremely angry, and he threatened to kill me if I were to come back again to a roadblock in Kruscica. I took the threat very seriously at that time, and that's why, on the 21st of June, in a United Nations' vehicle belonging to the High Commission for Refugees, that I went to Kruscica instead of using my own vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when he threatened to kill you if you went back to a roadblock in Kruscica, you're talking about if you went back to the roadblock in Kruscica through which you were trying to deliver humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was the roadblock that had been set up by angry civilians, it was the roadblock that I had to go through, in my opinion, in order to get to Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, if I could have the witness shown Exhibit 408?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, while the registrar is finding that exhibit, was the individual who threatened to kill you if he saw you again at the roadblock in Kruscica in this morning's video film that you saw?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was in the video film.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could put this picture on the ELMO, please? Just fold it back. You don't have to take it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is the individual that threatened to kill you depicted in this photograph with the No. 4 next to him?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, he's No. 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Colonel Morsink can you proceed to tell us about another incident that occurred where the HVO interfered with the delivery of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Another example where I was very closely involved was at the beginning of July 1993 in Busovaca, four trucks carrying humanitarian aid were stopped alongside the road, they were stopped by HVO soldiers. We heard about this incident that same evening on the telephone. The next morning, I went with a representative, Medicins Du Monde, doctors without borders, who was in two of the trucks. We went to the Busovaca police commission -- station where we were told that the unloading platform for the merchandise was not ready yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct. The cargo lists were not correct.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The bill of lading was not there. After a long discussion with the police commissioner, we were authorised to release the drivers, and after a lot of talk, apparently we were authorised to get back some of the load that was on that list. In the end, the police commissioner said to us that he would first consult with his chief in Mostar and that we should come back the next day in order to pick up the merchandise. The next morning, we set up a team of ECMM members, of the UNHCR, Medicins Du Monde, and a representative of the British battalion. We had tremendous problems in arriving at Busovaca. The regular road to Busovaca was blocked by big trucks, and on the other road, along the hills, or in the hills, there was fighting. At any rate, it took much longer to get there that way. When we arrived at the police station, the commissioner was already gone, and so we tried to get to the HVO brigade commander, and we were told that he had gone to see Blaskic in Vitez for a consultation. When we again went to the police offices after that, we met the brigade commander, Gorbasic, and he told us that the drivers, the merchandise and the trucks, would be given back when there was no longer any threats to Zenica. And that is why the roads were blocked, because there were threats, and I said to them that that was not acceptable, combining those two things was not acceptable. We then went to the HVO barracks to see whether the merchandise was still there. The merchandise had already been taken off the trucks, and we were asked to take the trucks and to get lost. We refused. We waited in the barracks until the police commissioner returned. After waiting for a long time, we received a written order from Mr. Gorbasic to take both the driver and the truck and -- the truck should be empty. We refused again. And then a few minutes later, a soldier arrived who threatened me with his rifle, and he told me that we had two minutes to get out -- ten minutes, no longer than that, and if I hadn't left in ten minutes, some bad things -- some very bad things could happen to me. Finally, with the drivers, we decided to leave, to disappear with the trucks. We stopped at the HVO headquarters in Busovaca. I lodged a protest, a very strong protest, and after that, we went to the police offices, and there too I lodged a protest very vigorously. Finally, I was able to get back safe and sound with the drivers and with the trucks to Zenica. The load of the two trucks, that is, there was equipment for the physicians in Zenica, from Medicins Du Monde, among other things there was medical material for all of that in one of the trucks, they were trucks that belonged to Medicins Sans Frontiers, and the last truck was carrying 20 tonnes of powdered milk for Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Shortly after the merchandise that you've just described was stolen, did you see it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The powdered milk is something I saw in the buildings, in the barracks, and some of the medical equipment, I saw some 13 microscopes also in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did the doctors at the hospital in Busovaca say in respect to the stolen aid that they had received?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: My monitor colleague talked to me about it and explained that they had enough materials -- rather, they did not have enough people to really deal with that, they did not really have anyone to deal with that type of material. They had 13 microscopes, but only one person, one sole operator to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said that the aid itself was owned by Medicins Du Monde; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, one part of the load, yes, was from Medicins Du Monde.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Also Medicins Sans Frontiers?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't catch the third organisation that was sending this aid?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: ECF, which was sending powdered milk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have Prosecutor's Exhibit 225 put on the ELMO, Mr. Dubuisson? It's a photograph. Give me just a minute, please, Mr. Dubuisson. I've obviously made a mistake on the photograph number. Could I have in the meantime Exhibit 419 placed on the ELMO? It should be a photograph as well, Mr. Dubuisson. Would this be the next ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be document 420, it's the photo we had on the screen a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges if you can identify that particular photograph and tell the Judges if this particular individual was involved in the incident involving the theft of the aid, humanitarian aid, that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The man in the photograph was an HVO brigade in Busovaca. He was the commander of that brigade, and his name is Dusko Grbasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am looking for an additional photograph. Let me ask you another question. When you met Grubesic in the police station, he linked return of the aid with the removal of a particular roadblock. Did he say where he had received those orders to make that kind of a linkage?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He stated that he had received word from Blaskic -- he said if he didn't (inaudible) them, he couldn't do anything, and that the threat would be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The English translation is not coherent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please? We have difficulty to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He said that he received an order from Blaskic to only remove the roadblock if the threat had been eliminated, and he had also received as an order to turn back in the trucks only after the border had disappeared. That is to say, only to reduce this roadblock after the trucks had been returned. So when the threat had been eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That apparently is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, the Defence is not in agreement with the interpretation, so I think we have to take this again, this being very clear, so that the Defence will be able to carry its own -- Mr. Hayman, you have the floor right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One other concern. Counsel stated that there was a linkage between the delivery of the aid and the removal of a roadblock implied by the BiH army in one of his questions two or three questions ago. That has never been testified to by the witness, and so I wanted to state that for the record. Perhaps it can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a suggestion, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, perhaps you may clarify. This is a very important point. You've made a link between the statement made by the witness, between the removal of the roadblock and the order given by Mr. Blaskic. So let's be very clear on this and make sure this is very clear for the Defence and he can also exercise his rights. Please, Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I make a request? Perhaps on this particular point the witness can answer the question in English. It might expedite this answer, and the witness can sense --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel, perhaps you might explain this in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will explain it in English. We had to deal with an HVO roadblock at the Strane or the Busovaca junction, the Busovaca T-junction at the factory. It was an HVO controlled roadblock and the four trucks in Busovaca were stolen by HVO soldiers. The order, as we were told by Grbasic, came from Blaskic to link the roadblock, the lifting of the roadblock, and giving back the four trucks, to link those two items together, and we said we do not agree with that, the roadblock doesn't have anything to do with giving back the four trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Now, Mr. Dubuisson, if I could have Exhibit 255? That is the correct number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the roadblock was an HVO roadblock, not a BiH --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was an HVO roadblock. It was put there because it was thought there was a threat from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 225 is indeed a death certificate. If you would like to specify what you're looking for, perhaps I will try to find it? So this is document 255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Twenty-five or 255?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Apparently this will be 255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Apparently, Mr. Registrar? Very well. Is it apparently or is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, do you identify the man on the right-hand side of that particular picture?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, the man who is at the police commission in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not fully correct. He introduced himself as the commissioner --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, that's not exactly correct. He is the one who presented himself as the police commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is the man, the policeman, with whom you dealt on the stolen aid convoy?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what is his name, sir? Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think his name is Ljubasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have the next exhibit, which is a special report dated the 4th of July? The subject is the HVO Busovaca stopping of NGO trucks and taking the cargo. The exhibit number is, Mr. Dubuisson ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be document 421.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this exhibit has a French translation attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Morsink, briefly, we won't go into detail on this particular document, but do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, this is a report which I have written.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You have written this report. Does this report reflect the events that you've just testified about, that is, the stolen convoy of aid that was looted at the HVO barracks in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, we wrote about this entire episode.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to turn to another subject, and that is an individual by the name of Zute. Did you have contact with an individual by the name of Zute?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I had one meeting with this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges about the circumstances under which you met Zute?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: In the evening of the celebration of Bajram in July, General Alagic and his group were attacked on the road, and a large amount of their personal weapons were stolen. He called upon the commander of the BRITBAT and also on the European observers or monitors and on the local commanders of the HVO and the BiH army, and during this meeting, it was decided that the following day Mr. Alagic and myself would go and meet with the believed perpetrator, Mr. Initic (phoen). Mr. Zute was believed the person responsible. The following day, we went to the headquarters of the HVO in the northern part of Travnik, and there, Mr. Alagic and myself, met with this person, Mr. Zute. The brigade commander was also present there, the commander of the brigade, it was a Mr. Leotar, and afterwards, after a long discussion, Mr. Initic said that he would return the equipment. And then, in that same afternoon, all of the equipment was returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was this man Zute described by the HVO as somebody who was one of the "uncontrolled elements" in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, he was described as an uncontrolled element, as a criminal even.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you meet with that individual on the 2nd of June, 1992, just to make the date precise?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. However, it was on the 1st of July. It was the following day. The Bajram holiday was perhaps on the 1st of July -- my memory is not very good on the actual date of that holiday -- the 1st of June, rather, or the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the HVO frequently use the excuse, when crimes were committed, when houses were burned, when houses were looted, when Muslim civilians were killed, that those events were the result of people who were uncontrolled elements? Was that a frequent excuse used by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it was said quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that this individual by the name Zute was under the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, he came to attend these meetings, and I think he came to follow the orders so, yes, I believe he was under some form of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If there was a group of 20 or 30 individuals who were known to be committing crimes in Central Bosnia, who were uncontrolled elements, in your experience and your observations, did Colonel Blaskic have the resources, soldiers, and sufficient police, to eliminate those "uncontrolled elements" at any time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I believe that they had so many soldiers and so many police that it should have been no problem at all to control a small group of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Having seen the scale of damage that you saw, scale of damage to Muslim villages, the loss of life to Muslim civilians, the cleansing of civilians from the municipalities of Busovaca, Kiseljak, and Vitez, the use of systematic use of forced labour, do you believe that those crimes were perpetrated by "uncontrolled elements?"

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I believe that one or two minor cases may have been committed by small, uncontrolled groups, but the large-scale and systematic manner in which these events took place, entire villages being burned, and other villages, we saw that it was the Muslim houses that were systematically selected, and we saw that the same type of events were taking place at the same time period in different locations, and it would be impossible, in my opinion, for this to have been carried out by uncontrolled groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to another subject area, if I could, and Mr. Dubuisson, could I have the next exhibits, which are three commands issued by General Blaskic marked in order, starting with the order that has the number 441 in the upper left-hand corner as the next exhibit followed by 443 and 444?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So document 441. This would be document 422.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I need to interrupt you one moment. Looking at the organisation of this, we're going to take a break at 4.20, and you said that you would be with this witness until four o'clock is that not right? Rather, you were expecting four hours for this witness, but I see now that you have already had two hours, we resumed at, let's say, 3.00, fifteen minutes to 3.00. Do you think you might be able to finish with this witness by 4.20, and I'll ask the Defence whether or not he feels he will be able to finish with his cross-examination before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not believe so, in all candour, Mr. President. We have been given a number of long documents we haven't seen before and there are matters in the documents we need to question the witness about in addition to his extensive oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I don't want to put too much pressure on -- too much pressure on the interpreters, I know they are tired, but I think the witness will have to return, and at that point he will return for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters unclear whether the last statement made by the Judge needed to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would note that these three exhibits are exhibits that have not yet been submitted for official translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, would you look at Exhibits -- would you look at the three exhibits in front of you, that should be 422, 423, and 424. Do you recognise those exhibits?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise them, but the numbering is not the same, 441, 443, 444. You did not say that in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't have the same numbers here. Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, these are the references which are given in the original documents and not the references that the registrar has given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. There is some connection between the two. I see. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When I'm referring to the numbers 422, I'm referring to the Exhibit number and not the number in the order that appears in the left-hand corner --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I have all the documents you spoke of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you receive those documents at BRITBAT?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you also receive these documents in conjunction with the previous exhibit I showed you, Defence Exhibit 141?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to -- and you received them in the form in which they appear before you, that is, there's an English translation, and a Croatian language version of it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So you received both versions.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like you to take Exhibit 422, please, which is the order number 441, and ask you, first of all, from where was this particular order issued?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It was at the headquarters of the operational zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was this an order that was initiated on -- from reading of this order, was it initiated on General Blaskic's order or was it something that he was doing as a result of some other situation that had developed in the theatre?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This is based on an order which came from high up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this document that is in front of you in the form of a command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I am reading. It says "I command." In my mind, that's a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you turn the page to the distribution list on the lower left-hand corner, and would you kindly read in English the distribution list of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Distribution. First, all the HVO brigades. Second, all the independent units under the command of the HVO 3rd operational zone commander (MTD TV LTRD 4th military police Bat., Vitozovi, Trvtko II, and Zuti).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the witness a question. You read 4 military police but. Is it but or battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't read that very clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's maybe the copy. It could be "battalion." It makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What do you think it is as a military man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's "battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In comparing the Croatian language version with the English language version, there appear to be nine items on the English version, English version, and ten items on the Croatian version; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you please place that order, the Croatian version, so number 10 appears on the ELMO? Could the ELMO be illuminated? And could the interpreters please read number 10?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The number 10 in Croatian says; "for the implementation of this command, all the brigade commanders responsible and those of independent units."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. You can take that from the ELMO again, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, first I'd like to draw your attention to item number 2 on that, and is that a command or an order that every subordinate commander, independent HVO unit commander, should issue commands to his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it asks for everyone to obey the orders and also submit their reports -- submit orders to their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you take a look at item number 4. What does that require?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Every day, at 10.00, 10.00 or 9.30 -- I can't read it quite well here -- all the brigade commanders and also the independent units are to send their special reports to the 3rd command of the operational zone. In these reports, it is important to refer to all the details in the military situation as well as all efforts that are being made in order to arrive at a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel, what was item number 2 and item number 4 suggest to you as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I would deduce this is a very clear order that would then be passed on to all the commands; therefore, there is a clear hierarchy here which exists. This is a clear order to present a report on the results of having carried out an order. I would deduce then that there truly existed a command structure and that there was very good control there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to item number 9 on this particular order. Can you read that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "All the HVO units are obliged by the Geneva Convention and its additional protocols, as well as all other instruments of the war law and the international laws."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you deduce from that that Colonel Blaskic was aware of the obligations under the Geneva Conventions, the additional protocols, and other instruments of the war law and international laws?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It's giving an order for everyone to follow orders. Therefore, he was aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This order, this command that is in front of you, was issued on the basis of a cease-fire agreement that was signed by Colonel Blaskic's superior, Milivoj Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to turn to the next order in front of you. It is Prosecutor's Exhibit 423, and it has the number 443 in the upper left-hand corner. Was this issued from the 3rd operation zone headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does Colonel Blaskic's name appear at the bottom of this particular command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you read to whom this order was sent, the distribution list in the lower left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Distribution: All the HVO brigade commanders, 4th battalion military police commander, special unit Vitezovi commander, special department Zepce commander, police station commanders in Busovaca, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Kiseljak, Fojnica, and Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, a couple questions. First of all, if you turn to the last of the distribution list and item number 3 in that exhibit, does it appear to you that Colonel Blaskic is issuing commands to police station commanders?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, he issues orders -- in this particular document does it appear that he's issuing a command or an order to areas that were not physically in contact with Vitez and Busovaca municipalities?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. The distance between Zepce was very long. In fact, you had to go through an area that was under the BiH army control, and to go to these various other villages was the same thing, Kiseljak, Kruscica. The order demonstrates that there were other contacts that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Morsink, does this particular order concern itself with forbidding the violent moving out of their houses the civil population?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you conclude from this order that Colonel Blaskic was aware that the forcible eviction of civilians was contrary to international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They don't mention human rights in this order, but it does say that it was forbidden to expel people by using violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was this order that was issued by Blaskic issued on his own initiative or was it issued as a result of something else?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He says in the beginning that it's based on the agreements at higher levels. That's what it says in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the Prosecutor's Exhibit 423 which has an order number 443 in the upper left-hand corner, and was that issued also from the third operational zone headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 443 or on the back 423 is what you just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 423 which is the Prosecutor Exhibit number, and in the upper left-hand corner is 443?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that issued from the 3rd operational zone in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does the name "Tihomir Blaskic" appear on the bottom of that order?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have the wrong exhibit. Would you now turn your attention to Exhibit 424 with the numbers 444 in the upper left-hand corner? Was that order an order that was issued from the third operational zone headquarters?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And does the name "Blaskic" appear on the bottom of that order?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does this appear also to be a command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It says on the top "The high command."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does this also have a similar distribution list to the previous orders?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Zute also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this an order dealing with the arresting of civilians and forbidding the arresting of civilians?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Also deal with forbidding putting houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does it deal with the protection of sacred objects, mosques, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's true also.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does it indicate that everybody who steals and holding of property shall be punished and solved through the normal disciplinary measures in courts?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was this order issued on the basis -- or was it issued on Blaskic's initiative or was it issued as a result of some other agreements?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's based on a cease-fire agreement issued from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you conclude from this particular order that Colonel Blaskic was aware that the evicting of civilians, putting houses on fire, destruction of sacred objects, and stealing property was illegal?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, he forbade that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to turn to another topic, if I can -- thank you very much. I'd like to turn to another topic, and that would be the subject of the use of civilians to perform forced labour, specifically trench-digging. While you were in Central Bosnia, were you aware of this particular practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was given protests, according to -- which said that civilians had been forced to dig trenches. I was given this during the meeting of the joint commission. During the meeting, I was made aware of 15 protests in that respect, 10 to 15, 10 to 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did both sides complain about this practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There were complaints about the HVO soldiers who forced the Muslim soldiers to dig trenches. That's how it always was said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really correct.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers forced Muslim civilians to dig trenches. The protest came from one side only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether or not the HVO, in fact, engaged in this practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There is one case to which I was a witness with HVO soldiers accompanying civilians who were carrying shovels, and who had to dig a hole or to dig trenches. When we asked the question of the local HVO commander in that respect, he felt that he had been a little bit cornered, at least that was the feeling that I had, that he was a bit cornered. He became very aggressive and did not allow me to speak with his soldiers or to the civilians concerned by the matter. And this incident was presented to the joint commission subsequently. This happened in May -- I think it was May, I don't quite remember anymore -- it was near Stranje. The military commander had a nickname, Marinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, two exhibits, please, Mr. Dubuisson. The first is a map, and if I could have the second exhibit also taken up to the witness as well as an aerial image? If you could give me the numbers on each, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 425 where the word "Vitez" is underlined in orange, and 426 is the big map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Colonel Morsink, Prosecutor's Exhibit 425 appears on the ELMO now. Did you mark the location where you observed this forced use of labour, forced labour by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you point out to the Judges where you observed the people who were digging trenches under the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's not easy to show you that on this scale, but it was in the north. We were coming from Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will get to that in the next exhibit. Can you just point on the exhibit that's before you, Colonel Morsink. You're pointing to an orange circle. Is that the area where you saw the Muslims digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It was that area where the orange -- which is the part which is circled in orange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then if we could take the next exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 426, and place that on the ELMO? Could you turn it the other way, please? Colonel Morsink, did I show you an aerial image and did I ask you to indicate on this particular aerial image two things: One, the direction from which you came when you saw the people digging trenches and did I also ask you to put a circle around the area where these people were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please go ahead and explain this diagram.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Here, in this region, Jelinak, the village of Jelinak, we were supposed to conduct an investigation because there had been some houses burned -- set on fire, rather. After the investigation, after we did it, we took this road, along this road. Part of the road had just been built. Here, at this point, rather high up, it was an elevated point, we met Mr. Marinac and his soldiers who had civilians with them. We tried to speak to him, but he was very angry. Afterwards, we continued along the road toward the Busovaca junction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, did you subsequently return to Stranje on the 13th of May with HVO representatives and did you meet with local Muslims who were still residing in the community?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We had a meeting at the Busovaca commission, regular ones, with both parties, and we tried to go on site with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you went on site to Stranje, on the 13th of May, what did the population, the local Muslim population, tell you had occurred to them with respect to trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They complained that on several occasions they had been forced to dig trenches. They also complained that many men from that area had been taken prisoner at the county prison and that the remaining men were forced to dig trenches. They were the men who had been taken out of the prison and ordered to dig trenches. While they were digging the trenches, several of them were wounded, some of them even died doing the forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at this location in Stranje, was there an HVO representative with you when those complaints were made?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, there were members of the joint commission on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there were a large number of complaints made at the local commission and at the joint commissions about civilian forced labour. Were those complaints being made in front of Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Mr. Nakic was present several times at various meetings, and he was spoken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those complaints also made in front and in the presence of local brigade commanders as well?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO Busovaca command was always there at that type of meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what was the response of the HVO in the face of these continuous allegations that civilians were forced to be trench-diggers?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: There were different reactions. Sometimes they said furious civilians had forced other civilians to dig the trenches and sometimes we were told that there had been abuses, that some had used HVO uniforms in an inappropriate manner, and on other occasions we were told that the HVO had already lost a great deal of ground and were therefore forced to have recourse to all type of reserve forces and that they had to call upon civilians to dig the trenches, and yet on other times there was no reaction at all. They just didn't answer the allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you also told that it was uncontrolled elements who were forcing civilians to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. That's what they meant when they talked about furious civilians. That's what they meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In addition to complaints that were made to the HVO at the local joint commissions, did other international organisations make complaints to the HVO about this pervasive practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The International Red Cross and the UNHCR were present at that those types of meetings, and I remember that Margaret Green from the UNHCR had protested because she had noted there were gypsies in the Vitez region who had been forced to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, Colonel Morsink, was Colonel Blaskic aware of this illegal practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He had to have been because his representatives were present at the meetings when we talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did the HVO ever take any action to stop this illegal practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No. I never heard of any kind of measures taken at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of a single HVO soldier being punished for engaging in this illegal practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, Colonel Morsink, why did the HVO engage in this practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think that it is dangerous to work on the front-line, and I think that they did not want to put their own soldiers in danger by forcing them to dig this type of trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn next, Colonel Morsink, to the issue of the intentional burning of civilian homes by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, it's twenty after four. We're going to take our break. You said four hours. You can do what you like, of course. You still have several days left. But I don't think that the cross-examination will be able to take place under proper conditions today. We're going to have to ask the Colonel to come back, and this will be counted against you. You have, if I'm counting correctly, one, two, three, four, five, five points to deal with -- is that correct? -- five points. In the meantime, I think the interpreters have to take a break, in fact everybody has to take a break, including the witness, we will take a good 20 minutes in order to rest up a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now continue. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, and Counsel, because of the considerable difficulties we have had today in using the procedures that have been devised, I have made a request of the Dutch government to make an exception of their general policy that Dutch officers are required to testify in their native language, and I have received permission from the Dutch government to allow Colonel Morsink to testify in English, and therefore, Mr. President and Your Honours, and Council we will now proceed with the Court's permission in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. First, I would like to turn to the witness. You do agree to that, Colonel, since you speak English very well, do you feel comfortable speaking in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This will therefore allow us -- thank you, Mr. Harmon, first of all, for having taken those measures, and I'd like to, through you, the Dutch authorities as well. This will allow us, since there are difficulties in having the interpreters come here to work in Dutch tomorrow morning, so that means we will be able to work the cross-examination this evening and to continue tomorrow as well which will safeguard the rights of the accused who -- for whom the cross-examination will follow the examination-in-chief. Very well. This does not mean that you can take more time than the time allotted to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, I would like to return to one topic about which there was considerable confusion before the recess, and that was you mentioned an HVO roadblock being linked with the return of humanitarian aid that had been taken by the HVO in Busovaca. Can you explain the linkage between the roadblock and the return of the humanitarian aid, please?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I can explain that. I'm sorry that I caused misunderstandings. I can point out the location of the roadblock at the map, at this map. The location at the roadblock was here in the area of the blue factory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Perhaps we could let the Dutch interpreter leave. Of course, it's your decision. Unless, according to the Dutch authorities, there is a litigious point here, but since you can't be here tomorrow. What do you think, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel, it is your presence at this point?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: If you agree, Your Honour, I would like her to stay here for a while, just in case I don't find the right English words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But tomorrow it wouldn't work that way because tomorrow we will be able to continue. That's what he said. Which means that you're going to stay, and we're pleased about that. But we will continue working with you tomorrow without a Dutch interpreter. I want to say that we will complete our work -- the work, including the cross-examination, by the end of tomorrow morning. Excuse me for interrupting. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: So the location of the roadblock was here, it was an HVO-controlled roadblock, and it was put there, told by the HVO brigade commander, because they were afraid of an attack coming from Zenica towards Busovaca. So the linkage that has been made was that the HVO commander asked us to take away the threat from Zenica, and if that threat was taken away by us, by ECMM, then they would be able to lift the roadblock and to let go the trucks, and that linkage was not accepted by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Now let me turn to the issue of the intentional setting afire of Muslim houses. First of all, were complaints made to the HVO by the ECMM and other international organisations about the intentional burning of houses, of Muslim houses, by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, they were made several times during several meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion did the HVO engage in the systematic burning of Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think so, yes, because the burning of houses was done very systematically in several places. They burned all Muslim houses. In other places, where the population was more or less mixed on an equal basis, they only burned the Muslim houses, and it was in another way systematically done because it happened simultaneously in different villages, around Busovaca, around Vitez, and in the same period around Kiseljak. So that requires quite an organisation, to do it in a way like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, did you visit the villages of Ahmici, Nadioci, Preocica, Sivrino Selo, Gacice Gomionica, Gromiljak, and Rotilj did you inspect the damage to Muslim houses in those villages?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I visited almost all of them you named except for Gomionica since I was not allowed to go in there. I visited all the other places and what I saw there was that almost all Muslim houses were burned, in some places they were all burned or 100 per cent of the Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And are you able to distinguish between battle damage and non-battle damage in respect of those burned houses?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think I am able to distinguish between battle damage and ordinary fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what were the -- how were the majority of the Muslim houses damaged, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The majority of the houses was damaged by severe fire, maybe lit with petrol or gasoline, but they were damaged by fire and definitely not by artillery fire or something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you base your opinion on any conversations that you had with HVO commanders as well?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I remember a conversation quite well which happened at the joint commission Vitez with the brigade commander HVO Vitez president, Mr. Mario Cerkez, and he was very upset that the army of BiH was trying to get in new forces into Kruscica through the mountains, there's a small goat trail through the mountains, and he said that that should be stopped, and if not, he was willing to burn down all Kruscica. And I was really surprised by an outcry like that because he was an HVO officer, he was the brigade commander in the area, he was wearing his uniform, and I didn't expect an officer at all making a statement like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that statement made on the 24th of May, 1993, a matter of weeks after the burning of Ahmici and other villages in and around Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do not recall the exact date, but it was made several weeks after all the villages in the area had been burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you take that threat of Mario Cerkez seriously?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, he said it in a very clear way, and he was on duty when he said it, he was an active member of the local joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in your opinion, could all the burning that you've just described that you saw been committed by uncontrolled elements?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do not believe that all the burning was done by uncontrolled elements since it was done in a systematic way all more or less in the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, Colonel Morsink, was Colonel Blaskic aware of this illegal HVO practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He must have been aware of it since it was in his area of operation, and it was -- it was mentioned in several meetings where his people were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So complaints were made about it at the joint commissions where his designees were present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever, at any time while you were in Central Bosnia, ever hear of any HVO soldier being punished or disciplined for burning down a Muslim house?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, Colonel Morsink, why did the HVO engage in this practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think it was one way to clear the area of all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn your attention next to the forcible expulsion of Muslims from their homes and ask you if you can relate to the Judges events that related to the forcible expulsion of Muslim civilians from the village of Gacice.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The village of Gacice is in the area, in the vicinity, of Vitez, it was under control of HVO, and approximately 100 or 200 people living there were part of the Muslim community, they were forced to leave Gacice, they were brought to Dubravica, that is the T-junction in the road from Vitez to Zenica, they were brought there, we were told, with trucks, with cattle trucks, and they were asked to get off the trucks in Dubravica and they were told to walk towards Zenica through the frontlines. We got a report on this during one of the meetings in Vitez from Mrs. Margaret Green from the UNHCR, and we got similar reports from the British battalion on the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, let me stop you right there. Were these complaints also made on the 4th of May, 1993, at a meeting of the ECMM house where the ambassadors from Spain, France, and Britain were present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that Mr. Merdan was very upset when he got the chance to explain to these three ambassadors what had happened in the previous three weeks in the area of Vitez, and he called upon this example of Gacice as one of the newest examples of expulsion of Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the report that the HVO had forcibly removed these civilians or that other people had removed these civilians? What was the complaint that was made?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The complaint was made that they were forced out of Gacice by HVO and, as I recall it, the answer was that they were forced out by angry civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, who told you that? Did you go see an HVO commander, brigade commander, the following day?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I will have to look that up in my notes, if necessary. I'm not sure who told it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you take a look at your notes, please, refer to your notes of the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I read in my notes that on the 4th of May, at the joint operation command, the complaint was made by Mrs. Margaret Green and by Jorge, I forget his last name, he's a field officer of UNHCR as well. And on the 4th of May, we spoke to this item with the mayor of Vitez, Mr. Santic, and during that meeting, Colonel Stewart and Mrs. Clare Podbielski from the International Red Cross were present and I recall that also Colonel Blaskic was present and they were told at that meeting that -- as I recall it, it was told by the mayor of Vitez, Mr. Santic, that they needed the houses in the area of Vitez, all the available houses, to be able to house Croat DPs, displaced persons, coming from outside, so they made kind of a plan to use all available houses or to make houses available so that they could house Croats in their own region.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you continue to receive reports after this incident in Gacice that Muslims were being continually forced out of their homes by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Colonel Blaskic aware of this illegal practice?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Again, these allegations were made during the local joint commissions, and his subordinates were present during those meetings, so he must have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, while you were in theatre, did you ever hear of a single instance where an HVO soldier was arrested and punished for evicting a Muslim from his home?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, I never heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn briefly to your contacts with Franjo Nakic. You ever have occasion to socialise with Franjo Nakic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of my tour, I was invited by Mr. Nakic to say good-bye to him at his private house, and I met his wife there, we had a drink together for approximately one hour, I said good-bye, and the next day I left for the coast.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, if I could have two exhibits shown to the witness? The first is an aerial image and the second is this item which is a list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The aerial photo is 427 and the list will be 428.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please place 427 on the ELMO, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, can you identify what this particular exhibit represents and orient the Judges a little bit to the items contained in that particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the main feature you see on this aerial photograph is the location of the British battalion in the small town call Bila. Our house was on this side, on the upper side of this camp. This road was called by us the press road since a lot of houses were occupied by international press. And either in this circle or in this circle, I'm not sure, but I'm very positive that the house of Mr. Nakic was watching over on the fields on this side, either in this circle or this circle, there was this house where I met him at the end of my tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we have the next exhibit placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what that exhibit is?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: This is a list of names. These people were taking part in the joint command in Travnik that was established in the beginning of May, and this list is signed by Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan themselves, they were themselves members of this joint command in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does this list indicate where Mr. Nakic lived?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
