utterances.text: On number 2, it says Franjo Nakic and his function, deputy commander, his private telephone number, and the address says Stara Bila, and that's the area I pointed out on the map, that's known as old Bila, Stari Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me change the topic and ask you. What's your position of the command structure of the HVO, and can you tell the Judges in your own words, whether, in your opinion, Blaskic and his staff, his subordinate officers, had control over HVO forces in and around Vitez, Busovaca and Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think the HVO forces in the area, the operational zone middle Bosnia, were well-structured, since they had this operational zone level, I compare it to our division level, they had brigades under this division, several brigades under their control, they had separate units under their control, they had military police, they had divisional artillery under this operational zone command. The area of operations of their command was clearly defined, including areas like Zepce and Fojnica. That's for the structure of the organisation, the HVO organisation. I think they were capable in issuing orders. They had good telephone communications, they had good fax communications, and I saw several HVO officers carrying small portable radios, so I think also the communication part was well-organised. They controlled all the switching stations of the telephone lines, so they could, in fact, decide who was having connections, who not. I think they were well-structured in the way that they issued written orders in the military way, correctly-written orders, shaped in the right military way with proper addresses on it. They asked for reports in these orders, it's also another military way of organising things, you do not just order anything that you ask for a report afterwards. So I think that I can say that the HVO was well-organised, they had a good organisational structure, they were capable to command, to order things, and I think they were also capable to control since everything was reported in these local joint commissions, since they had good communication, the subordinates must have been able to report all their findings from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the HVO and Colonel Blaskic in particular have the ability to control what was described to you as "uncontrolled elements?"

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think this Djuti is the best example, to me. He looked like an uncontrolled individual, the way he was dressed; but, on the contrary, he immediately reacted on the invitation to come to a meeting, and he responded to Nakic, the second in command of this operational zone, and he followed the orders of Mr. Nakic by returning all the stolen goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Based on your experiences in Central Bosnia and what you saw, what conclusions did you draw in respect of what happened to the Muslim population in the areas controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: My conclusions were, and they were based on certain things I saw, they're also based on things we discussed at ECMM meetings at our headquarters in Zenica and they're also based on findings by other monitors, and the conclusions are that the HVO and/or the HDZ, I'm not sure, I think in combination, so the military leaders and political leaders, I think they made a plan to control the whole area where the majority of Croats lived, to really control it by expelling all Muslims, and they used tactics of fear, tactics of burning houses, tactics of killing Muslims, to scare the rest away, and they used, on the other hand, tactics of propaganda to pull in Croat minorities from other areas which they would not be able to control at all. So the incident of Gacice, where they tried to pull the Croats from that area into Vitez, and examples of Ahmici and Rotilj, around Vitez and Kiseljak, where they tried to expel all Muslims by killing, by burning, by fear, so I think it's a plan, and it was carried out as they planned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel Morsink. Mr. President, I have concluded my examination. I would now ask that items 407 through 428 be introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only have exceptions on a few of those, and they are exhibits that were not authenticated by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Those are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Not identified. Please, when you say authenticated and identified, they are very delicate terms. Please, first of all, tell us which ones you are talking about, which ones you have problems with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm looking in my notes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 417. 417. I have it before me now. It is the note signed by the accused, and it's an instruction, an order. Colonel, you recognised this document, did you not, this document 417? It is not the witness who wrote it, of course, but it corresponds to a time period in which he was on duty, 417. Could you identify this document?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do recognise this document, and I recall that I said it was handed out to me at one of the meetings, and I recall that I only said it wasn't signed by Mr. Blaskic himself since -- it might be a copy or a draft or a translation of the original order into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. Then, in that case, it is admitted. Now, 418; is that right? 418?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So let's go on to 418 then. I have the French version here before me. This is a letter or notes or a report written by Mate Boban addressed to General Mario, and it seems to me that the witness identified and made some comments about this. Colonel? Let's go back to that document, 418.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right, I identified the document because I was asked to read what is on it, and I'm not positive whether I got this order myself or whether I read it in the ECMM headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So long as he saw it at the time, I don't have an objection, Mr. President. But as to 416, 417, and 418, I did not have in my notes that he recognised these from the time of his service as opposed to being shown them yesterday in the Prosecutor's Office or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee you, Colonel, whether or not you saw it at the time, I don't know whether you recall or not, but I think perhaps it is important. Colonel, do you recall seeing it during your time of service? We're asking a lot of you now, but try to remember.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't think I saw this one in Zenica during my duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. But today can you identify this document as having been the reality of something issued by Colonel Blaskic at that time and addressed as a request for assistance? Let me see. Where is it addressed exactly? It's -- I see it's addressed to the UNHCR, to the European Union as well. Do you feel this would be a plausible letter given the fact there was also a fax attached to it, I believe?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I think we are talking about two different orders. The one I was referring to that I haven't seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 416, 416. 416 in front of me. Yes. What I have here before me is 416, a document signed by Blaskic and which is addressed to the High Commissioner for Refugees and also the European Union or Community, Nations, and also some Croatian members, and this is a request for assistance. Can you identify at least today before us this as something that's identifiable, in your mind?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I can identify this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's see. Very well. Now, whether or not you saw it at the time, Mr. Hayman, it's difficult to state, isn't it, difficult to ask a witness whether or not, several years later on, five years later, whether or not he has seen all of these reports. So I think perhaps it should be admitted. I'll look to my colleagues first, whether or not they have any comments. This shall be admitted as evidence. Mr. Hayman, do you have any other problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Those were the only three that my notes reflected the witness had not identified them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, Mr. Hayman. I hope that you know that it is now 5.20, and you have another hour or so to work on the cross-examination. Colonel, you're now going to be receiving questions from the Defence. Mr. Hayman, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good evening, Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you arrived in the theatre, you said you were briefed on the purposes and goals of the Busovaca joint commission. Were you told what events had given rise to the founding of the commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was informed by two colleague monitors about the Busovaca joint commission, and I was briefly informed by Remi Landry, the Canadian monitor, on what happened in the previous months before I arrived in theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Remi Landry tell you about the conflict in January in the Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He told me something about that. I do not exactly recall what was said, but it had to do with the conflict between HVO forces and army of BiH forces in the area of Busovaca, Kacuni, and Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you in substance that the BiH army had attacked, the HVO had the enclave from roughly Bilalovac to Kacuni and had expelled Croats from that zone in between those two locations?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he told me that at that event, but I at least was aware of that later on. I was told by several people that there had been fighting in that area, and as a result of that fighting, the area of -- let's say the HVO-controlled area Kiseljak and the HVO-controlled area of Busovaca were not linked anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So is it fair to say the purpose of the commission was, among other things, to implement and monitor the cease-fire that was reached after that January 1993 conflict in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think that was the main reason why the first Busovaca joint commission was raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, did you tell us when you first arrived in either the Lasva or Kiseljak valleys, what the date was?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The first day I arrived in the area of middle Bosnia was the night of the 16th, I arrived at the U.N. BH command in Kiseljak. I was taken with an ECMM car during the night through Kiseljak, Visoko to Zenica. I was briefed only for a few minutes at the first evening. I got my first proper briefing at the 17th. So that was, in fact, my first appearance in the area, the 17th in the morning, 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: On the evening of the 16th, did the EC monitors you were with, did they have an assessment of the situation at the time, or was there general confusion in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I myself did not get a clear picture at that time. I asked for a briefing, but everybody was very busy, and they seemed not to have enough time to brief a new monitor during that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In the car, did anyone tell you that they thought they knew what was going on and what was going on? Were you driven by another EC monitor on the night of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes, I was driven by a German monitor together with his interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether he had a clear understanding on the night of the 16th of what was going on or whether there was general confusion in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't know whether he told me that he had a clear picture. He was not able to bring it over to me. I did not have a clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The next day, did you go to the headquarters of the Vitez brigade of the HVO, that is, the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. I went there together with Eric Friis-Pedersen, the Danish monitor, he was in the area already for a long time, so he was more or less the head of the mission in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there fighting going on around that location at the time you went on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. There was shooting around the headquarters, small arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What building was the headquarters in at that time; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: As I recall, it was the cinema building, since, at the entrance, there were posters of films.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that is in reasonably close proximity to the Hotel Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: As I recall it, it was 300 or 400 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Colonel Morsink, when you respond, please turn towards the Judges, and when you are receiving questions, you can turn towards the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While you were meeting with personnel at the Vitez brigade headquarters on the 17th of April, did live rounds come in through the windows?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: All windows were covered with wood, and I recall that the wood on the windows in the hallway next to the room where we met, the wood was hit several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: By rounds from rifle fire, presumably?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Rifle fire, small arms fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether that was from the general direction of Stari Vitez or Old Vitez or from some other direction, if you're able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It was impossible to tell since the windows were all covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 407 could be provided to the witness, please? That is the order of appointment of personnel to the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I have it in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that it was your belief at the time, and this is dated the 1st of May, 1993, that Mr. Nakic was the deputy commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you agree with the following: Question: Prior to 16 April, 1993, did you believe Franjo Nakic to be the deputy commander of the HVO Central Bosnia operative zone? Answer: Yes. All of the documents at the time were signed, showed Mr. Nakic was the deputy commander. Indeed, I saw a document from 13 February indicating he was the deputy commander or at least as an individual representing Colonel Blaskic as a deputy commander. Question: After the conflict, be it the 16th or 18th or 20th of April, you concluded that Mr. Nakic was no longer the deputy commander but was the chief of staff; correct? Answer: Yes. And then there is additional narrative consistent with the answer "Yes." Am I correct then, that is not your understanding, that as a result of the conflict in the middle of April 1993, that Mr. Nakic lost his position as deputy commander of the operative zone Central Bosnia and became the chief of staff of that command?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the facts or the things you just read from your computer. I don't believe they were told by me -- sorry -- I don't really understand the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's not your testimony.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: -- where you would like me to answer you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking: Do you disagree with the statements I read to you, the question and answer I read to you? Do you disagree with it? That is, you believe that Mr. Nakic was the deputy commander on or about May 1st and at other relevant times all after the conflict in the middle of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do believe that Mr. Nakic was, when I arrived, the deputy commander of the operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, I'm reading -- I read from the testimony of Mr. Remi Landry at pages 7695 and 7696 of the transcript in this case.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I add as an officer, as a Dutch military officer, the position of deputy commander and the chief of staff? In the Dutch army, the deputy commander and the chief of staff are one person, so there's not a distinction in level, whether you're more important or less important. In the Dutch system, and I think it's the same in the Canadian system, the chief of staff and the deputy commander are the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could it be a promotion to be a chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Not according to our system. Maybe in another system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you about Exhibit 408, the videotape, and perhaps -- I'd like the technical room -- I haven't been able to coordinate this so far, but perhaps they could roll the tape and find a passage about a minute into the tape where one of the BiH army officers has a flag patch visible on his right shoulder? If they could perhaps queue that up and hold that for a question. Let me ask you, though: This tape, was it made of a local joint commission meeting or of the joint operative or operational command meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's not very clear since, during that period, the decision was made to organise the Busovaca joint commission, the old one, into an interim phase, an interim phase, the joint operational command in the same ECMM house in Bila; and after that, one or two weeks after that, we were asked to organise the four local joint commissions. So it's more or less like an interim phase. We ourselves called it the JOC, the Joint Operational Command or Joint Operational Commission, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know the date of the meeting depicted in the videotape, Exhibit 409?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I can look it up in my notes. I'm not sure when it was. I think it's the beginning of May or the end of April. More likely the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was present for sure. I'm shown on the tape itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who made the tape?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think the tape was made by ITN, since I got the whole recordings of ITN made during that period, and I think this is picked out of that original tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they tape the whole meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, they did not. At least I did not get that from ITN. I got the tape of all the recordings they made during my presence in the area of middle Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know the tape that was shown, is that the entire ITN tape, or was it edited?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it you did not prepare the tape; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, we saw in the tape Mr. Nakic, you pointed out Mr. Nakic, as well as Mario Cerkez. Would Mario Cerkez have been attending a meeting of the joint operational command or only of the local Vitez joint commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Only the local commissions would be attended by the local brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Such as Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Such as Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Does that suggest to you that that was a meeting of the local Vitez joint commission?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right. But as far as I can recall it, the real local joint commission Vitez was not active at that time, so it's really an interim phase, starting up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Nakic and Mr. Merdan attended some of the local joint commission meetings for a few weeks but then generally did not attend such meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That is correct. They attended, I think, approximately three weeks most of the local joint commissions in Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, and after that, they asked us to continue the work, and they told us that they had to be present in the joint command in Travnik, in the PPT building in Travnik, since that joint command was active after those three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And thereafter they were not able to attend the local joint commission meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think that's the reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, the tape, Exhibit 409, also depicts officers from both warring parties being escorted home or back to residences or other offices. Is that similar to the type of escort, if you know, that was provided on the 17th of April, 1993, to Marko Priscalo (phoen), and Zoran Pilicic (phoen), two HVO officers who were shot while entering or about to enter going from an UNPROFOR Warrior to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that incident, but this -- carrying people in armoured cars was meant to bring them through frontlines because there was still fighting around the British camp, so we had to bring in the HVO officers in armoured vehicles, and the army of BiH officers were not able to go through HVO-controlled area without protection, so that's the reason why BRITBAT offered to support us in these local commissions and they offered to transport these people in armoured cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And, similarly, when the joint commission teams went out and did their work in other areas, HVO officers were not able to travel without ECMM and UNPROFOR support; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, but the meetings in Kiseljak took place at the base of the Canadian company in Kiseljak, at Camp Padberg (phoen), so they only asked for armoured cars for the army of BiH side. And the same thing happened in Busovaca. There, we had most of the meetings at the headquarters of the Dutch transport battalion in Busovaca itself, so also that only required the transport of the army of BiH officers into Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm allowing the translators to complete their translation, and that was why I'm making an awkward pause between answer and question. On those occasions when Mr. Nakic went to Kiseljak, for example, for a local joint commission meeting there, he would have to be transported in an UNPROFOR Warrior; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That is correct, but several times he came with us in our armoured Mercedes since that was comfortable and safe enough to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And you were able to get through the BiH army checkpoints en route to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Most of the times, we were able, since Mr. Merdan travelled with us as well and he was able to lift any roadblocks if they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether any other meetings of the joint operational command or the local joint commissions were videotaped?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't think that other combined meetings were videotaped. I know of some separate meetings we had during this shuttle diplomacy phase that were taped but then only one side was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I cannot see, Mr. President, into the technical room. Perhaps if they have been able to locate this still image, they could put it on the video monitor? If it doesn't appear, then the answer will be "No," and I'll proceed in another fashion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much to the technical personnel in the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have before you, Lieutenant-Colonel, a still from Exhibit 409, the videotape. First of all, there is a gentleman seated who takes up about the left 50 per cent of the screen. Do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That is Mr. Sivro Sivet. He was the local commander of the army of BiH forces in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the patch on his right shoulder?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes. That is the German national flag, and it's part of, let's say, a German shirt that was used by German soldiers in the '60s and '70s, so it's a uniform part used by the Dutch army (sic) in the '60s and '70s.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said the Dutch army. You mean the German --

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I mean the German army, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Sivet, at the time he wore this uniform, he was not a member of the German army, he was a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. That's the way he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn that it was common practice for soldiers on both sides of the warring factions in Bosnia to wear whatever bits of decent uniform they could get their hands on, and that sometimes included patches of the armies of foreign nations? Did you come into such information in addition to the image on Exhibit 409 which you've just seen?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I recall that I saw a lot of these examples on the army of BiH side. They told me that they were short of uniforms, and I recall that I only saw a few of these examples on the HVO side. They were normally, let's say, military properly-dressed soldiers on the HVO side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes the use of that tape, and I again thank the technical booth.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think it would be useful to give a number to this since -- we could perhaps give the number of D144 to that photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, a still can be produced of that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let me direct your attention forward in time to a meeting you described on April 19, 1993, with Mario Cerkez concerning the truck bomb incident. Do you know what happened to the physical evidence of the truck bomb, i.e., the truck chassis and any other physical evidence at the scene?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to that. The only thing I recall seeing myself was part of the engine of the truck laying next to a large hole on the road, and I don't know whether the rest of the truck was moved during the explosion to the side of the road or whether it was removed by anybody else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This location, this was a location within Stari Vitez, within BH-controlled portions of Stari Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this part of town is called Stari Vitez. It was very close to the mosque, some 200 metres from the mosque, and it was quite close to the area of Stari Vitez that I later found out was controlled by army of BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there any attempt, if you know, to form a joint investigation of the incident that would combine information available to the BiH army, the HVO, and international organisations to try to investigate the truck bomb incident?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any attempt to form a combined task-finding mission. I recall that we asked Mario Cerkez to investigate this matter, and he promised us that he would do so. So as I recall it, there was no need for an extra investigation party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the issue with Mario Cerkez again, or was it only mentioned on one occasion, this issue of an investigation into the truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not personally discuss it with him again since I was a young monitor at the scene. Eric Friis-Pedersen was the one who did most of the speaking and I was just taking notes, and after a few days, I was team leader but then busy in other areas and other jobs, so I don't recall that it was asked or raised again, this question. I did not do that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And it was not done in your presence, is that correct, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. It was not done in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you said, I believe, you met the next day in the Hotel Vitez with a group that included Colonel Blaskic, is that correct, on the 20th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. A joint -- Colonel Bob Stewart and Mrs. Clare Podbielski, since they planned to go to Colonel Blaskic and they asked me to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What time was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not sure. As I recall it in my memory, it was the beginning of the afternoon. 1.00, maybe 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In whose office was the meeting held?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The meeting was held in the Hotel Vitez, so that's the headquarters of the operational zone Middle Bosnia, and as I recall it, we went through the hall where the HVO guards, and then opposite to the entrance, on the other side of the hall, there's a large room with, I think, large brown seats, and that's where we spoke to Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any recounting of this meeting in your notes or diary?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think I do. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I have notes that it happened on the 20th of April. I'm not sure whether you asked me if it was on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, I asked about the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The 20th. I've got notes on the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What do they reflect?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They reflect the meeting we had with Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: How was Colonel Blaskic identified in your notes, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, I just put his name in. I was informed by Bob Stewart that Colonel Blaskic was the commander of the operational zone Middle Bosnia, so as I recall, it excited me that I was to meet the highest commander in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember meeting him on that day? Do you actually remember sitting down face to face with Colonel Blaskic on the 20th of April, 1993, or could it be a mistake?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's hard to say. I remember the excitement meeting the highest commander, I remember entering the headquarters, I remember passing the guards in the presence of the British battalion commander who I admired already after a few days, and as I recall it, I was introduced to the upper commander, as far as my knowledge goes. That was Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please look at him in the face, General Blaskic. Is this the man you met on the 20th of April, 1993, in the Hotel Vitez? Do you recall that? Or are you not sure?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's hard to say. You see so many faces in the first two, three days, in the middle of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If you had and if Colonel Stewart had chewed out Colonel Blaskic concerning the truck bomb as you described, is that something you would have put in your daily operational report, attending such a meeting, meeting the commander of the operative zone for the first time, and witnessing this rather dramatic, perhaps, exchange, between the British battalion commander and the HVO operative zone commander? Is it something you would have put in your daily operational report?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think later, when I was in the area for already several weeks, I would have. But according to this incident -- I was not in charge. Colonel Bob Stewart was in charge. He was the one who did the talking. He introduced me or asked me to come with him, together with ICRC, so it was not a proper ECMM meeting, so there was no ECMM need to report to Zagreb about this meeting, as I recall it now. Later on, I would have reported on more than just my own meetings, but since I was not in charge and I was still a young monitor, in my third day on the scene, I can understand why at least I did not report this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What about when you were interviewed over six days by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in 1996, an interview which resulted in a 23-page single-spaced typed statement? In that statement, there is a discussion for over about a third of the page of your meeting on the 20th of April, but there's no mention of Colonel Blaskic, no mention of a meeting with Colonel Blaskic, and no mention of any comments by anyone else, including Robert Stewart, directed at Colonel Blaskic in connection with the truck bomb or otherwise. Isn't that something that would have been discussed over the course of six days of interviews and recorded in a 23-page single-spaced typed statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection to that, Mr. President. That's not a proper question, whether it would have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you asked over those six days of interviews to describe your meetings with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you asked, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, the objection has been sustained, to the Prosecutor. You cannot ask the question where you have the statement made by the Office of the Prosecutor. You have analysed it, you have drawn certain conclusions from it, but you cannot go beyond that. You know exactly the conditions under which the witness was questioned. Please, if you would like to ask another question, but please reformulate your question. Rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I will rephrase it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Over those six days, were you asked to describe your meetings with Colonel Blaskic and did you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was not specifically asked to describe meetings with Colonel Blaskic. I was asked to describe anything I remembered from the period I was in the area of Middle Bosnia. So from the 13th of April until the 13th of July. You must understand that this was the first time I was debriefed on these three months. I stayed in Germany for two years, did my German course there, I worked at the army staff for more than one and a half years, and then suddenly somebody from the Tribunal comes and debriefed me for the first time, and it's really very hard to get back all these memories from such a long time ago. I used my small notebooks, my big notebooks, I used my diary to recall things as good as possible. And, of course, more memories come back. They even come back now when I speak. Like, for instance, the colour of the furniture. It's just something you remember all of a sudden how a certain situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then tell us, with your refreshed memory, what did Colonel Stewart say in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: As I recall it, Colonel Stewart was really very upset that the HVO and HDZ accused the Brits of being partial, being partial in just evacuating Muslim homeless people, homeless because of the car bomb. He told about alleged people being thrown out of trucks, British trucks and British Warriors, and he told us that -- or Colonel Stewart was very upset that he was accused of being impartial (sic) since the British battalion were the only ones to give aid to those people, they were the only ones to give help during the evacuation after the car bomb, and he was very upset about the accusation that they were impartial. So he asked again, "Where was your organisation to help? What did you do to help the homeless people? What did you do to help the wounded people? Why was HVO not there? Why was the local organisation not there?" So that was the main point of the meeting, his anger about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The lack of a response?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, counsel. There appears to be an error in the transcript and I'd like to correct it before it rolls up. It says the following, it says: "Colonel Stewart was very upset that he was accused of being impartial." You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel, thank you. I agree, there's an error?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I meant "partial."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You meant partial or the record should be that he was upset at being accused of being partial?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, counsel. In sum then, quickly, and we'll move on, Colonel Stewart was angry at the lack of a response to the situation in terms of helping the victims, the homeless, the wounded, and he was angry at both the residents of Stari Vitez and at the HVO for not responding better; is that correct? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't think so because he would not show his anger about the Muslim side, I think, when he met Colonel Blaskic, and according to my knowledge, the Muslims did not have control in Vitez, so they were not able to organise any evacuation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the BiH army was not in control of Stari Vitez; is that your understanding at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I know that they were in control. Later on, I found out that they were in control over part of Stari Vitez, but I don't think they had the opportunity or the means to evacuate a large number of people out of this endangered area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: At the time of this conversation, I take it the effort to assist the wounded, evacuate them, was completed; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: As far as I know, the British battalion took out all the homeless and wounded people and the dead were recovered a few days afterwards, also by BRITBAT.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let me ask you about the subject of propaganda. You mentioned both the HDZ, H-D-Z, and the HVO. What channels did the HDZ use for putting out propaganda?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was told that they used radio and television, local radio and local television, and since I cannot understand the Croatian language, I was told by interpreters on duty with the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you ever told that Colonel Blaskic had made any inflammatory or ethnically prejudicial or derogatory remarks on TV, radio, in speeches or otherwise during your tour of duty? Did you ever receive such information?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You did not. What channels did the HVO utilise, in your view or judgement, to disseminate propaganda?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say whether they took influence on the local radio and local television, but the same message was spread out, and it was supported by HVO officers like, for instance, as liaison officer at the headquarters of the operational zone in Vitez, he was the one who told me that Guca Gora was in flames, he was the one who told me that thousands of Croats were forced to leave the area or fled in the direction of Novi Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This is Darko Gelic you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's Darko Gelic I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When he made those statements to you, was he speaking to a room thronging with reporters, or was he having a personal conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He was having a conversation with me, and there were more monitors present and my interpreter was present, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was there anyone from the news media present?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of two examples of the use of propaganda, Zenica and Guca Gora. Aside from the documents that have been discussed first regarding Zenica, do you have any information of any other propaganda put out, not by the HDZ but by the HVO, concerning the status of Croats in Zenica? Anything else? Anything to add?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The status of the Croats in Zenica was mentioned more than once in the local commissions of Vitez and Busovaca at several meetings several times. Even into the middle of May, I recall that during several meetings, the positions of Croats in Zenica was discussed again and again, and these meetings always started with large accusations from both sides that their own people were harmed in another area and that it should be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the press -- I'm sorry. Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm finished, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was the press present at these local commission meetings that you've described?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The press was present at several local commission meetings. The Vitez local press was there, as I recall it, at two or three meetings, and the local Busovaca press was present at more than five or six meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would they attend the entire meeting?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: They would be there the entire meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was that deemed conducive to the work of the local commissions?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We thought they could support us because every meeting was -- we finished every meeting with a mutual statement from both commanders, an official statement, signed and written about the attempts we made during the meeting and about the agreements we made and the things we would try to do the following days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You spoke of a particular radio broadcast which said it was safer for refugees, I believe refugees in Grahovcici, to go to Vitez and Novi Bila than to return to the Zenica municipality. Is it your opinion that at the time that was not correct, that it was either safer for the refugees, Croat refugees, to go back to Zenica or that it was equally safe for them to be in the Vitez enclave or to be in the Zenica municipality? What exactly is your opinion in that regard?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: As I told you, as I told the court, we made an investigation in this first phase together with this Catholic priest from Zenica, we made an investigation in all these villages, and we together came to the conclusion that it was safe for people to return. We broadcast it or we told our conclusion to the HVO representatives in Grahovcici, to the Croats -- let's say the oldest people of the community, of the refugees there, and we told it to the Catholic priests in Grahovcici as well, and they all agreed with our conclusion that if we said so and if Father Stjepan said so, since he was well-known priest in the area and he was loved by everybody, if that was his judgement, then people would believe him and it would be safe to go to their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The radio broadcast you quoted, though, said it was safer for refugees to go to Vitez and Nova Bila than to return to Zenica. I take it you don't agree with that. You believe it was either safer or just as safe for Croat refugees at the time to return to Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The essence of the broadcast was more than that, not just the matter of safety. The essence was that it was propaganda, that lots of Croats had been massacred in the area of Zenica and that their houses had been burned and that it was no longer safe or not safe or unsafe, or whatever word you would like to use, for them to go back to their own houses and they were told to go to Nova Bila and to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You visited Grahovcici on approximately the 8th of June, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Grahovcici was earlier. That was the 25th until the 27th of April. The 8th of June was the Guca Gora incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very good. 25th to 27th of April was Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'll look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could you just check and make sure?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The 24th of Zenica -- the 24th of April, I stay in Zenica and go to Grahovcici for the first time, and I finish the Grahovcici job on the 26th of April, so it's the 24th until the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In your estimation, how many Croats had been murdered in the Zenica region by that point in time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did an -- we paid some visits to the areas where the people fled from, together with Father Stjepan, and we were told that -- I'm not sure how many there were. I would have to look it up in the report I made. But I think some 10 or 15 Croats had been killed in that area, and I read in another report made by two other monitors in the previous days, they did an investigation on similar incidents in more or less the same area but not in all the same villages I went to, that another number of Croats had been killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And houses burned? Half a dozen? A dozen? Five dozen?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I would say between 10 and 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And houses looted? 50? 25?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think more -- I think -- I'm not sure. I didn't count them all myself, but I think it must have been some 50 houses looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 295 could be placed before the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: This, Lieutenant-Colonel, is a special report on Croats in Zenica dated 20, 21 April, 1993, produced by the ECMM RC Zenica and authored by three of your colleagues, and I'd like to call your attention to several portions of it. There is a French translation of this exhibit, Mr. President, 295A. In paragraph 1, as a result of a visit to certain areas in the municipality, your colleagues reported that the military section of the Zenica prison had more than 200 Croat prisoners, half military and half civilian. Down in paragraph 2(a), they report that in the village of Cajdras they found four houses burned, 38 empty. In Veternica, three burned houses. In paragraph 2(d), a village that was shelled. Paragraph 2(f), Stranjani, seven burned houses and most of the 240 Croat homes were robbed. Paragraph, 2(g), Zahalie, eight burned houses, four killed Croats. Paragraph 3(c), Zalje, at least 25 houses were burned. The Father, referring apparently again to Father Stjepan, I believe, told us that in that village were killed 10 civilians, including a 90-year-old man and a three-year-old girl. And then the report concludes that this was less damage than had been expected, less killing than had been expected, less burning, less looting than had been expected. Would you agree, Lieutenant-Colonel, that the Croats in Zenica at this time in April, they did have reason to be concerned for their safety?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: If this is all the facts and if Croats knew about this, then I believe that they were afraid, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Blaskic at the time, he's down in the Vitez area -- correct? -- his headquarters is in Vitez, was at the time?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did he have a way to get to Zenica to make a personal appraisal of the situation, or would he have been blocked at the BiH army front-line from going to Zenica to inspect these different villages where only 240 houses were looted in one, only 10 civilians killed in Zalje, et cetera? He didn't have that kind of information, did he?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Probably not at the 20th or the 21st. But since we reported through ECMM and in the local joint commissions what our findings were, he must have known that afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is, he must have known that the numbers in Exhibit 295 were accurate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, I did not report on this special report ECMM, since when this report was written, I was in Vitez myself, and the daily and special reports were discussed in the ECMM meetings in the evening, at that very day, and I came back to Zenica three days later, so I did not discuss this report myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Are you surprised by these numbers? Does this sound like more killing, more burning, more looting than you had the impression occurred against Croats in Zenica during the latter half of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was told by Lars, who is one of the authors of this special report and who went with me the last day I went to Grahovcici myself, it was reported by him that this was the case, but we did not face it, all these villages ourselves, and we put effort on some of these villages, and we had the impression, and Father Stjepan had the impression, that all people could go back to their own houses. We spoke to the neighbours still there, we spoke to some Croats that were still there in their own houses, and they told us, "Please ask the people to come back." So that's what we tried and that's what we arranged with all the buses. And there were HVO soldiers present, HVO local commanders, and they could have reported what our findings were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did they? You don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't know whether they did or not, but the broadcast came, and that's why they took away our buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They got excited, these local commanders, and they commandeered your buses; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: The local military police, the HVO military police took away our buses, and after a certain time, we were able to speak to the local HVO commanders again, and after a while, they agreed in still going back to their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the HVO Vojn Policija, military police, took the buses, then you spoke to the regular HVO local commanders, and after some period of discussion, they were successful in helping you get the buses back; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct, and meanwhile, the buses were once used to bring the people to Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about Colonel Blaskic personally -- and we'll get to the documents that have been discussed in a moment if we continue that long tonight -- other than the documents, can you tell us anything about Colonel Blaskic's involvement or lack of involvement in the issue of either returning Croats to Zenica or allowing Croats to leave Zenica if they wished?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I didn't meet Colonel Blaskic very often, and I didn't have the opportunity to speak to him personally. I was present at a number of meetings where he was. But, on the other hand, using his name with brigade commanders, using his name at local commissions always gave me the impression that he was honoured by his own subordinates. Using his name put more weight on the scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you use his name to get the buses back?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't recall that, that I used his name then, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, in speaking of Guca Gora -- Your Honour, I'll try to complete the Guca Gora questioning, perhaps ten minutes, if that's satisfactory to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In discussing Guca Gora --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have until 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Fine. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In discussing Guca Gora, you talked about Alagic and said Alagic was roughly of the same rank as Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What was Alagic's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: As far as I know, his area of responsibility was the whole Travnik area, including places like Guca Gora, Novi Travnik, way uphill.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was he responsible for Zenica as well, or was that the third corps' responsibility?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: He was not responsibility for Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Alagic was under the third corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Whereas Colonel Blaskic, although he might not have had the rank, he was responsible for the entire terrain on paper at least, Lasva Valley, Kiseljak Valley, and other areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You said that Alagic went with you to Guca Gora, but Colonel Blaskic never went with you anywhere to investigate allegations. Did you ever ask him to go anywhere with you and investigate allegations?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not ask him personally, but then I didn't ask Mr. Alagic to come. He offered himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: When you went to visit Alagic, would he almost always offer you a drink, liquor, whiskey, something like that? Is that a fair generalisation?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: No, he hardly ever did. I recall only once having a drink with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very well. With respect to the action in the area of Guca Gora, what was the BiH army trying to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think they launched an attack from the northern area into the region of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They were trying to link Zenica and Travnik, were they not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. They needed freedom of movement. They needed the road under their control from Travnik to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have told us that the church at Guca Gora was not touched in the course of that action; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct. I visited that church myself after the fighting passed from the north across Guca Gora in a southern direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: And that neighbouring Croat communities, no wanton destruction or attack on civilian structures by the BiH army, or was there such conduct in the Guca Gora region generally?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not see any proof of that during that visit to Guca Gora, and an investigation was made the day after by Philip Watkins, and there was a special report made on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 296, which is a map, could be placed on the ELMO, and Exhibit 414 be provided to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now, you have before you on the ELMO, and you should be able to see it on your video monitor, on Exhibit 296, this is a map including the area of Zenica and villages to the west and south-west of Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you see, towards the middle upper portion of the photograph, the village of Dolac, D-O-L-A-C; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn your attention on Exhibit 414 to paragraph 1, "General Situation." This is the second page, not the cover letter. The next-to-last sentence, commencing with the next-to-last sentence which reads: "UNPROFOR further report the Croat village of Dolac as deserted and over 100 houses burnt. The number has not been confirmed by ECMM, although there is evidence of some houses still burning." Is that information -- and the date of this is the 8th of June, 1993 -- when was your visit to Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Just a second. My visit was at the afternoon of the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So the same day that you visited Guca Gora, UNPROFOR reported that there were 100 burnt houses in Dolac and that the Croat population was absent. Would you agree that's what Exhibit 414, paragraph 1 reflects?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: It says so in the same report, but I'm not sure whether we were aware of this fact when we visited Guca Gora or whether we heard it at the evening briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll call your attention, in fairness you don't need to see it, but it's Exhibit 415, paragraph 8, reflects that of those visited villages, the worst is Dolac which has approximately 15 to 20 burnt houses, and then lists burnt houses in smaller numbers in other villages. This is dated 19 June, 1993, indicating that about eleven days later, there was better information that only 15 to 20 houses in Dolac had been burnt as the BiH army advanced from Zenica towards Travnik. Now let me ask you about the documents you reviewed, beginning with Exhibit 415. Do you have 415?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, it reflects that the number of Croatian families to leave their homes in the Travnik area varies from between 5.000 and 20.000. Is that also the information you had on approximately the 8th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: We didn't have exact numbers or not even estimations about the number of Croats. What we saw was large groups of civilians carrying their -- I think the belongings they could take, walking in a southern direction through Novi Bila in the direction of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 of this exhibit reflects a discussion of the allegation of desecration of churches and states: "The church in Travnik has been badly damaged internally with the organ and artifacts smashed. The Guca Gora church was free of any damage when initially visited but since has been extensively damaged internally. The Dolac church was hit by a single mortar round, but this is not assessed as a deliberate attack." Did you go back to the church at Guca Gora and see in what ways it had been desecrated and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I did not myself. Mr. Philip Watkins and the other monitor, Torbjorn Junhof they made the second report, they made the investigations on allegations that there was more damage than we saw in the first check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If Exhibit 416 could be provided to the witness. This is called a "Call for help" from then Colonel Blaskic. First I'd like to direct your attention to the original B/S/C version of this report, that's at the back. Do you see that copy?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: You mean this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. In other words what we used to call Serbo-Croat. Do you see a small stamp about two inches down from the left-hand side of the document?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: A small square stamp with the date on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: A small square stamp in a different type, different type set, from the rest of the document. It includes a large rectangle that is cut into certain rows and so forth. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Now let's look at the English translation and perhaps, unless everyone has a copy, we can put this on the ELMO. I don't know, Mr. President, if I can proceed without having it on the ELMO, if it is confusing. Please interrupt me if it is confusing any of Your Honours. On the face page, and I will be working from the English, do you see the translation of this stamp indicating -- would you not agree -- that this document was received in Kakanj on or about the 7th of May, 1993, and it's a received stamp of sorts. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What happened to the HVO in Kakanj; do you know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you know where this order came from? The Prosecution provided it to the court. Do you know where they got it?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: Well, it was addressed to the European observer mission so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but this copy that they have is stamped received HVO brigade, the Kostromanac (phoen) brigade in Kakanj. How did they get that copy, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't know. We were able to go to Kakanj -- I didn't receive it myself, but we were more or less free to move in certain areas so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The BiH army attacked the HVO in Kakanj and drove them out during your tour of duty, did they not?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I was not working in that area, so I'm not aware of it. I know that there was fighting, of course, but I'm not familiar with the exact order of fighting and what happened exactly in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that if there was such an attack on or about the 12th of June, 1993, and 5.000 Croats fled Kakanj, those who did not fled (sic) were imprisoned in a camp, that that's the kind of information --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness has testified he does not know about Kakanj, so this question calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has criticised the "Call for Help," which is Exhibit 416, and authored by my client. I'm asking him if that kind of information would affect the thinking and the psychology of anyone responsible in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm not at all criticising what you have said, Mr. Hayman, I understand the objection of the Prosecutor as well, but I'm not criticising your question, I simply wish or think that perhaps you should rephrase it calmly, try to rephrase it, rephrase your question, very quickly and with conviction and firmly, and this is -- should be done so that the witness has some time because I believe you spoke about the attack in June 1996 or in May 1996, and -- 1993, correction, 1993, and so if you could ask your questions -- I'm not criticising the way you're asking questions but I see you're asking vehemently and very strongly, but could you please try to ask your questions calmly and quietly, because here it is very difficult for us three to understand exactly what you're looking for. Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would also object to the question because Mr. Hayman is asking about events that he says took place on the 12th of June, 1993, which is five weeks after the call for help was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I don't see how I could accept your objections. Well, I am in the process of asking Mr. Hayman to rephrase his question to see whether or not his newly rephrased question is acceptable or not. I see we're almost at the break now -- Mr. Hayman, would you please rephrase your question but please be careful because it seems we're dealing with events in June or in May, so what exactly is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Mr. President, and I'll hold the issue of Kakanj for Exhibit 417 which is dated the 14th of June and specifically references 10 to 15.000 Croats exiled from Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Staying with Exhibit 416, it says, in the first paragraph that,"Colonel Blaskic feels the need and responsibility to inform you once again about the difficult position of the Croats in Zenica who have been living in total isolation for quite some time." Would you agree with that statement, that the Croats in Zenica at that time, 4th of May, 1993, had been cut off and were living in Zenica, isolated from other communities of Croats?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I think that's correct, they were isolated from other communities, but since the priest was free to move and to visit his parish, I think it's a different kind of isolation. They were not free to go to places outside Zenica, I think, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you think it's a fair statement, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I don't think they live in total isolation. As I experience an expression like that, "total isolation" is more than just having to stick to your own town because they were able to shop, they were able to move from one house to another, they were able to go to the church, to visit their priest or the priest was able to visit his parish in Zenica. Of course, they were not totally free, but they were also not totally isolated, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It says on the next page, the letter states that by blocking and isolating the Croats of Zenica, the food supply for the 4,500 Croats of the Zepce and Usora region have also been blocked. Was that true, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: HENDRIK MORSINK
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the food situation in Zepce. I know that there were problems to reach Zepce, but there was a mixed population north of Zenica, so they had to -- they had food problems for everybody, if there were any food problems, and if they wished to get transport through, then they had to bring transport through for both groups of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this would be a convenient breaking point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think we should stop now. We've asked a great deal of the interpreters and everyone is tired. We've also asked a great deal of the witness. I'd like to remind you we only have tomorrow morning in session so the witness will return tomorrow, I'm sorry, but we will have to resume tomorrow. I believe you're going to be finishing your cross-examination tomorrow, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will be able to finish it by the conclusion of tomorrow's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Because I don't think perhaps it will be necessary to call another witness tomorrow, but that's up to you to decide, Mr. Harmon. You know my ways and the ways of this Chamber, so then we will all meet tomorrow morning at 9.45. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 6.32 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of July, 1998, at 9.45 a.m. 22 23 24 25
